cases.abstract: ConvNeXt revisits the performance gap between conventional convolutional networks and hierarchical vision Transformers by updating training and architecture without introducing attention. Starting from ResNet, we first strengthen the training recipe and then hold it fixed while progressively changing the network at approximately controlled computational cost. The resulting design separates spatial and channel mixing: large depthwise kernels operate at a narrow width before pointwise layers expand and contract channels, making broader spatial processing affordable. Evaluations compare similarly sized Swin models on ImageNet classification, COCO detection and instance segmentation, and ADE20K semantic segmentation. At 384 x 384 resolution, ImageNet-1K-trained ConvNeXt-B achieves 85.1% top-1 accuracy against Swin-B's 84.5%, alongside V100 inference throughput of 95.7 versus 85.1 images per second. Scaling both model size and pretraining data yields 87.8% for ConvNeXt-XL after ImageNet-22K pretraining and ImageNet-1K fine-tuning at that resolution. Competitive downstream results show that the revised convolutional backbone is useful beyond classification. These results support a convolutional alternative for the evaluated recognition tasks without shifted-window attention or relative position biases.
cases.methods: ConvNeXt makes large spatial kernels affordable by applying them before channel expansion. A 7 x 7 depthwise convolution mixes locations independently in each channel; two pointwise convolutions then expand the width fourfold and restore it, separating spatial processing from channel mixing. Keeping the depthwise operator at the narrow input width limits its cost, while the pointwise layers supply channel capacity. Each residual block retains one GELU and one layer normalization. Separate stride-two convolutions downsample between stages, but this change initially caused training to diverge; normalization at resolution transitions stabilized the revised design. Architectural changes are accumulated from a ResNet baseline under a fixed 300-epoch AdamW recipe with augmentation and regularization, retaining the same hyperparameters. FLOPs remain approximately controlled, and small-model accuracies average three training seeds. This sequence assesses architectural changes after the initial training gain, but each comparison remains conditional on earlier modifications.
cases.results: ConvNeXt-B's classification results show that retaining convolutions need not trade accuracy for throughput relative to Swin-B. With ImageNet-1K training and 384 x 384 inputs, top-1 accuracy is 85.1% versus 84.5%, and V100 inference throughput is 95.7 versus 85.1 images per second, at 45.0 versus 47.1 GFLOPs. This is not the best accuracy across all tested configurations: EfficientNetV2-L reaches 85.7%, with 480 x 480 inputs and 53.0 GFLOPs. The downstream comparisons test whether the redesigned backbone remains useful beyond classification. With ImageNet-22K pretraining and Cascade Mask R-CNN, ConvNeXt-B reaches 54.0 box AP and 46.9 mask AP against Swin-B's 53.0 and 45.8. Under the same pretraining regime, UperNet evaluation on ADE20K with 640 x 640 crops and multi-scale testing yields 53.1 versus 51.7 mIoU. The gains against Swin therefore extend to localization and dense prediction, even though the ImageNet-1K-trained EfficientNet model retains the higher classification score.
cases.notes: Retained the training-versus-architecture distinction, attention-free block rationale, scaling result, and downstream contribution. Main classification comparisons use Table 1; downstream comparisons use Tables 3 and 4. Section 2 ends at 82.0% for ConvNeXt-T; Table 1 lists 82.1%. The revision does not reconcile them. Sequential changes are conditional on earlier choices, not independent component effects. V100 classification throughput is distinct from A100 COCO FPS.

cases.abstract: Reconstructing a photographic scene for interactive viewing requires both tractable fitting and fast rendering. We represent static scenes as anisotropic 3D Gaussians initialized from sparse structure-from-motion points, with spherical harmonics encoding directional color. Their geometry can adapt during optimization, while direct projection into splats makes the representation accessible to a differentiable tile rasterizer. Cloning, splitting, and pruning redistribute primitives as fitting proceeds; shared depth sorting accelerates approximate opacity blending without imposing a fixed limit on gradient contributors. Evaluation covers 13 real scenes and synthetic bounded scenes. At 30,000 iterations, averages across the three real-scene datasets range from 134 to 154 frames per second at native image resolutions on an A6000, following roughly 27-42 minutes of training. Reconstruction quality is competitive with Mip-NeRF360, but not uniformly better: on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, SSIM and LPIPS improve while PSNR remains lower. Interactive rendering is obtained at a substantial storage cost relative to neural radiance fields, with artifacts in poorly observed regions and occasional popping remaining practical limitations.
cases.methods: The rasterizer avoids two costs that would make explicit splats expensive to train: sorting separately for each pixel and storing a variable-length history of blended contributors. It assigns projected Gaussians to 16 x 16 pixel tiles and sorts keys combining tile identity with view-space depth in one GPU radix operation. Pixels traverse the resulting tile lists from front to back, accumulating color and opacity until saturation. Backpropagation revisits those lists in reverse and recovers intermediate blending information from final accumulated opacity, avoiding individual contribution lists while retaining gradients for all contributing splats. This makes the rendering path usable for optimization at varying depth complexity, rather than accelerating display through a fixed gradient cutoff. Rendering losses update geometry, opacity, and spherical harmonic color alongside gradient-guided cloning and splitting. Because each tile shares one depth order across its pixels, blending remains approximate.
cases.results: Real-time rendering does not require uniformly superior image metrics. On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset at 30,000 iterations, Gaussian splatting improves SSIM from 0.792 to 0.815 and LPIPS from 0.237 to 0.214 relative to the published Mip-NeRF360 scores, while PSNR is lower, at 27.21 versus 27.69 dB. It renders at 134 frames per second on an A6000 after an average 41 minutes 33 seconds of training, but stores 734 MB of parameters against the baseline's 8.6 MB. The practical gain is therefore interactive display at competitive quality, purchased with substantially greater storage. A separate Truck ablation tests whether fitting could be accelerated by limiting gradient contributors: at 30,000 iterations, restricting gradients to the ten frontmost splats lowers PSNR from 24.81 to 13.84 dB. This failure supports retaining gradients through the blended sequence rather than assuming a cutoff preserves quality. High frame rates nevertheless coexist with occasional popping and reconstruction artifacts where training views provide poor coverage.
cases.notes: Kept the original quality-speed-storage argument and gradient-cutoff test; omitted the early-stopping comparison to connect the renderer's design more directly to its ablation. Table 1 supplies dataset averages and stored-parameter sizes. Mip-NeRF360 quality scores on its dataset come from the original publication. Its reported 48-hour training budget combines four A100 GPUs used for 12 hours; no matched-A6000 training speedup is claimed. Table 3 uses separately downsampled images, so its Truck scores are not pooled with the main evaluation. Stored-parameter size is not peak training memory, which can exceed 20 GB.
